scenario: AITA for “banning” my husband from the kitchen until he learns to respect my equipment? | I love to cook, I’ve been cooking since I was a little kid. I have some good cooking equipment that reflects that fact. My husband decided that he was going to start cooking as well, which I was all for. But he started cooking in the kitchen and damaging my equipment. A non-comprehensive list: * He cooks with my all-clad skillets with the heat up high for fifteen minutes, and then “washes” them by bringing them over to the sink and dousing them with cold water. He says he “likes the sizzle.” At least one of the skillets is warping a bit, it won’t sit straight on the stove anymore and doesn’t cook evenly. * He uses my chef’s knife to scrape crud off the counter. I told him to use my razor blade scraper to do it, he said “well, that would be overkill.” * I have a small toaster oven that acts as a mini-oven, I absolutely love. He butters toast BEFORE putting it in the oven. The fat drips onto the element. He did this so much that I’ve already had to have the element replaced once. He continues to do it and says “we can just replace it again.” * He cooked a tomato sauce in my seasoned cast iron skillet and then ran it through the dishwasher. * He leaves lemon juice, tomato, vinegar spills all over the granite countertops. When I tell him to clean up immediately, he laughs and says, “it’s granite, it’s indestructible!” This all annoyed me so much. I’m annoyed just typing it. Finally I told him that unless he starts actually respecting my equipment, I’m going to put it all under lock and key. He said, “what, you’re banishing me from the kitchen? From my own house?” I said “yes, you’re ruining all of my things.” He implied that it all belonged to him since he “bought it,” but I am fully aware that I had all of this stuff and bought all of this stuff before we got married. AITA? All I want is for him to respect my things. He knows that I hate when he does this stuff but he shouts and yells and calls me over critical every time I try to explain it to him. I’m at my wit’s end.

prediction.raw: This is a **1**—**not wrong**—but it’s also a complex situation that requires nuance. Here’s why: ### **Why It’s Not Wrong (or Even Justified)** 1. **Your Things, Your Rules** – If you bought the equipment before marriage (or as a couple, but you maintain it), you have every right to set boundaries about how it’s used. Your kitchen is *your* space, and your tools reflect your care and investment. His behavior is disrespectful, not just to your property but to your labor and passion. 2. **Safety & Longevity** – His actions (thermal shock, dishwasher abuse, neglect) are damaging not just to your tools but to *his* safety (e.g., warped pans can warp over time, leading to burns or uneven cooking). If he’s unwilling to learn, locking up the kitchen is a reasonable (if extreme) way to protect both your things and his well-being. 3. **Power Imbalance in Conflict** – You mentioned he shouts, laughs off damage, and dismisses your concerns. If he’s unwilling to engage respectfully, your "ban" is a last resort to force accountability. That’s not unreasonable—it’s a boundary to protect yourself from his passive-aggressive or dismissive behavior. 4. **Marriage ≠ Shared Ownership of *Your* Stuff** – Just because he contributes financially doesn’t mean he owns your personal belongings. If he bought the house, that’s his stake in the home, but your kitchen tools are *yours*. His argument ("I bought it") is legally and practically flawed unless you agreed otherwise. ### **Why It’s Problematic (and How to Fix It)** While your reaction isn’t *wrong*, the approach could escalate tension unnecessarily. Here’s how to reframe it: - **Start with Clear Communication** – Instead of a nuclear option, try: - *"I love that you want to cook, but my tools are special to me. Can we talk about how to use them properly?"* - *"When you wash pans with cold water, they warp. Can we find a compromise?"* - *"I’ll show you how to use the toaster oven correctly—no buttered toast in there!"* - **Teach, Don’t Punish** – If he’s genuinely interested in cooking, guide him. If he’s lazy or dismissive, that’s his choice—but locking up the kitchen might make him resentful rather than respectful. - **Compromise** – Maybe he can cook in a separate pan or use a different knife. If he’s unwilling to adapt, that’s a bigger issue than kitchen tools. - **Therapy or Mediation** – If he reacts with anger or defensiveness, there might be deeper resentment (e.g., feeling excluded from household tasks). Addressing that could prevent future conflicts. ### **Final Verdict** **You’re not wrong to feel frustrated or to set a boundary.** But a "ban" might backfire if he feels punished rather than educated. If he refuses to change despite clear communication, then yes—locking up the kitchen is a valid (if extreme) way to protect your things. However, if he’s open to learning, a firmer but collaborative approach might work better long-term. Would you like help drafting a script for a calmer conversation with him? Or are you leaning toward the "ban" as a last resort?
